briefings.title: Demis Hassabis, Alison Noble and Paul Nurse discuss the future of science with AI

people.name: Demis Hassabis
people.role: Nobel Prize Laureate & Co-founder, Google DeepMind

people.name: Alison Noble
people.role: Professor of Biomedical Engineering, University of Oxford

briefings.tldr: Artificial intelligence is driving a monumental shift toward "science at digital speed," enabling researchers to bypass decades of manual labor through computational breakthroughs like AlphaFold.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR** 
Artificial intelligence is driving a monumental shift toward "science at digital speed," enabling researchers to bypass decades of manual labor through computational breakthroughs like AlphaFold. While this transition promises a golden age of scientific discovery, it requires urgent global collaboration to solve the AI "alignment problem," navigate the rise of general intelligence, and preserve creative human inquiry in the lab.

## Science at Digital Speed: The AI Impact So Far
* **The AlphaFold Breakthrough:** In 2020–2021, Google DeepMind used AlphaFold to predict the structure of all 200 million proteins known to science in approximately one year. 
    * *Immediate Solutions:* AlphaFold was highly accurate and capable of folding an average protein in just a few seconds.
    * *Democratizing Global Access:* In partnership with the European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL), the database was made open-source. Today, over 3 million researchers from 190 countries use these structures via simple keyword searches, eliminating the need for expensive wet-lab equipment.
* **The Three Pillars of Digital Speed:** Demis Hassabis defines the rapid evolution of science through AI across three dimensions:
    1. *Computational Speed:* Resolving highly complex molecular structures in seconds instead of years.
    2. *Rapid Dissemination:* Bypassing the traditional 10-year timeline for physical experimental methods (like CRISPR) to permeate the scientific community.
    3. *Agentic AI:* Moving into an era where AI doesn't just process data but actively generates scientific hypotheses and designs experiments.

## The AI-Assisted Laboratory and the "Virtual Cell"
* **Eliminating Laboratory Drudgery:** Paul Nurse emphasizes that a vast majority of wet-lab work consists of repetitive tasks like pipetting. AI is already transforming daily lab efficiency:
    * *Image Analysis:* Processing complex biological imagery now takes minutes instead of days.
    * *Literature Surveys:* Large language models can consolidate massive amounts of scientific literature in seconds to jumpstart research.
* **Fostering Creative "Taste":** Freeing PhD students and postdocs from manual lab tasks allows them to focus on high-level intellectual work, such as choosing the right questions, establishing rigorous controls, and formulating innovative hypotheses.
* **The 30-Year Dream of the "Virtual Cell":** Hassabis and Nurse discuss the long-term goal of simulating a living cell to understand life’s complex emergent behavior.
    * *The "Sloppy" Biology Challenge:* Nurse warns against trying to simulate cells using rigid physics-based calculations (e.g., hundreds of differential equations), noting that cellular processes are naturally "floppy and sloppy." This plasticity is precisely why adaptive, deep-learning models are better suited to biology than traditional math.
    * *Incremental Simulation:* Hassabis proposes modeling smaller, self-contained sub-units—such as the cell nucleus—as a pragmatic starting point.

## Navigating AGI Timelines and the Compute Divide
* **The Singularity Horizon:** Hassabis states that society is currently in the "foothills of the singularity," predicting that Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)—systems that surpass human-level capability—is only a few years away.
* **The Science vs. Engineering Gap:** Market forces have accelerated commercial AI engineering (such as consumer chatbots and LLMs) faster than the scientific community can analyze how these "black box" neural networks function.
* **The Academic Compute Divide:** Alison Noble notes that academic researchers struggle to compete with massive tech firms spending tens of billions on high-performance computing. 
    * *The Open-Source Solution:* Hassabis suggests academic researchers should bypass the "fear of missing out" on building frontier models. Instead, they can utilize smaller, highly capable open-source models (like Google’s Gemma 4) which are small enough to run on a single laptop but match the frontier capabilities of the previous year.
    * *Restructuring Academic Rewards:* Noble highlights that current academic publishing cultures penalize scientists who slow down to deeply analyze and stress-test AI systems, prioritizing being "first" over scientific depth.

## Existential Risks, Alignment, and Philosophy
* **Four Core Post-AGI Risks:** Hassabis identifies the key societal challenges of superintelligent AI:
    * *Bad Actors:* Rogue states or individual bioterrorists weaponizing general-purpose AI.
    * *The Alignment Problem:* The unsolved technical challenge of ensuring autonomous systems remain constrained by human-designated guardrails once they surpass human intelligence.
    * *Economic Inequality:* Ensuring the massive wealth and medicinal benefits generated by AI are distributed equitably to all nations.
    * *Human Meaning and Purpose:* Resolving the philosophical crisis of human identity when machines can outthink humans.
* **De-conflating Intelligence and Consciousness:** Hassabis argues that consciousness and intelligence are separate properties. He advises utilizing AGI first to study neuroscience and better define what consciousness actually is before attempting to cross the "second Rubicon" of building conscious machines.
* **A Renaissance for Philosophy:** The panel emphasizes that philosophy of science is more critical than ever. New ethical frameworks, virtue models, and epistemological tools are urgently needed to help humanity define "understanding" when relying on complex, un-provable AI simulations.

***

## Notable Quotes

> "We're in the foothills of the singularity... AGI is only a few years out now. And society's had a lot of time to sort of have advanced warning of this. I think it's time for all of us to take this more seriously." 
> — *Demis Hassabis*

> "Our motivation is curiosity about the unknown. Frankly, the tools we use... are important, but I don't think they change the character of that fundamental aspect of science, which is understanding the world." 
> — *Paul Nurse*

> "Big data is the problem, AI is the solution... AI is the perfect description language for biology, just like maths was for physics." 
> — *Demis Hassabis*

briefings.title: Full interview: Trump says Iran ‘is not an endless war’ as conflict reaches 100 days
briefings.tldr: In an exclusive Meet the Press interview, President Donald Trump declared that the U.S. is on the verge of a deal to end its 100-day military conflict with Iran, while aggressively defending his economic policies, proposed payouts to J6 defendants, and disputed election claims before abruptly cutting the interview short.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
In an exclusive *Meet the Press* interview, President Donald Trump declared that the U.S. is on the verge of a deal to end its 100-day military conflict with Iran, while aggressively defending his economic policies, proposed payouts to J6 defendants, and disputed election claims before abruptly cutting the interview short.

---

## The Iran Conflict and Peace Negotiations
* **Military Status:** President Trump characterized the 100-day-old conflict (Operation Epic Fury) as a "military exercise" and "blockade" rather than a war. 
    * **U.S. Casualties:** Trump noted that the U.S. has lost 13 service members, comparing this favorably to high-casualty historical conflicts like the Vietnam War.
    * **Troop Presence:** Approximately 50,000 U.S. troops deployed in the region will remain there until "completion" because keeping them stationed there costs very little and they may still be needed.
* **Degraded Iranian Capabilities:** Trump claimed that the U.S. military has "decapitated" Iran's military leadership and destroyed its naval, air, and anti-aircraft capacities.
    * He estimated that Iran has only 21% to 22% of its missiles left and that most of its drone manufacturing and launch pads have been destroyed.
    * He asserted that Iran's underground nuclear enrichment facilities were totally obliterated by U.S. B-2 bombers and are currently buried under collapsed mountains.
* **Negotiation Status & Leadership:** Trump stated that the U.S. is "very close" to a deal, mediated in part by officials from Pakistan.
    * **New Interlocutors:** The U.S. is negotiating with a "third group" of Iranian leaders, including the severely injured son of the former Supreme Leader, whom Trump described as "more rational" and "brave."
    * **Key Deal Terms:** Trump is insisting on strict language that prevents Iran from not only "developing" but also "purchasing, acquiring, or buying" nuclear weapons. 
    * **Sanctions Leverage:** Trump stated he will not unfreeze any Iranian assets or lift sanctions upfront; economic relief will only occur after Iran complies with the deal.

## Economic Outlook, Agriculture, and Federal Reserve Pressure
* **Monetary Policy:** Trump expressed strong support for newly appointed Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh but actively campaigned against potential interest rate hikes.
    * **Economic Philosophy:** Trump argued that economic growth does not cause inflation and that raising rates "penalizes" success. He advocated for lowering rates to incentivize further industrial expansion.
* **Support for Farmers:** Addressing reports that 70% of American farmers are struggling to afford fertilizer, Trump asserted that "farmers love me and the farmers trust me."
    * He cited the $28 billion aid package he provided to farmers during his first term (funded by tariffs on China) as proof of his commitment.
    * **Energy Prices:** Trump promised that once the conflict with Iran is finalized—either via a signed agreement or final military action—domestic gasoline and fertilizer prices will "drop like a rock," aiming for gas prices below $1.90 per gallon.

## The $1.8 Billion "Anti-Weaponization Fund" and J6 Defendants
* **Fund Objectives:** Trump defended his proposed $1.8 billion Anti-Weaponization Fund, which is currently blocked by courts and faces bipartisan opposition in Congress.
    * **Compensation Targets:** Trump stated the fund is designed to financially compensate individuals whose lives, families, and livelihoods were "destroyed" by the Biden administration's justice system.
* **January 6th Payouts:** Trump suggested that J6 defendants—including some of the 172 individuals who pleaded guilty to assaulting police officers—should be eligible for taxpayer-funded compensation.
    * **Conspiracy Claims:** He claimed J6 defendants were "ushered into the building" by FBI agents and pleaded guilty only out of fear of facing 15-year prison sentences.

## Clash with the Press and Abrupt Termination
* **Election Integrity Claims:** Trump reiterated unsubstantiated claims that the 2020 presidential election was "rigged" and claimed that current vote counting in California is "crooked" because state officials take multiple days to tally votes.
* **Interview Walkout:** When interviewer Kristen Welker pointed out a lack of evidence for his election fraud and J6 conspiracy claims, Trump attacked Welker and major media networks (NBC, ABC, CBS, and CNN) as "dishonest" and "crooked" before ending the interview early.

---

## Notable Quotes

> "I don't consider that a war, but if you want to define it as such, I guess you can. I don't define it at all. I don't think about it. I just do what I have to do."
— **President Donald Trump**, on whether the naval blockade of Iran constitutes an act of war.

> "They've conceded the fact that they will not have nuclear weapons... I want to put the word 'if they buy or purchase or acquire,' you know, you've got to have that in there too because that's not developing."
— **President Donald Trump**, on his specific negotiation demands for a new treaty with Iran.

> "My feeling is that when a country is doing well, they shouldn't be penalized by immediately raising interest rates. They should actually be incentivized."
— **President Donald Trump**, on Federal Reserve policy.

> "All right let's call it quits because I've had enough. Thank you darling, have a good time... A country can never be great with a dishonest press."
— **President Donald Trump**, abruptly ending the interview with Kristen Welker.

briefings.title: How AI Is Transforming Healthcare, Biotech and the Future of Medicine

people.name: Morgan Cheatham
people.role: Partner & Head of Healthcare and Life Sciences, Breyer Capital

briefings.tldr: AI is transforming healthcare from an art into a computational information science, driving massive efficiencies across diagnostics, clinical trials, and patient care.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR** 
AI is transforming healthcare from an art into a computational information science, driving massive efficiencies across diagnostics, clinical trials, and patient care. To capture this value, innovators and investors must navigate a complex regulatory landscape, bypass fragmented legacy data oligopolies, and prioritize immediate, high-utility business models over purely theoretical science.

---

## Redefining Medicine as an Information Science

* **The Healthcare Data Paradox:** Despite the U.S. spending 20% of its GDP on healthcare and generating one-third of the world's data—including complex medical records, lab results, imaging, and omics data—patient outcomes have not improved proportionally over the last 10 to 20 years. 
* **Key Acceleration Drivers:** Morgan Cheatham, M.D., highlights three core pillars driving the modern healthcare investment thesis:
    * **Computation:** Transitioning medicine into a highly structured information science rather than a subjective clinical art.
    * **Precision Medicine:** Moving away from standard "one-size-fits-all" blockbuster drugs toward tailor-made therapeutics designed for specific patient mutations.
    * **Prevention:** Prioritizing tools that keep patients healthy rather than simply treating them once they fall ill.
* **Reducing Administrative Friction:** AI is not replacing doctors or nurses; instead, it is absorbing back-office friction and non-clinical tasks, allowing providers to focus directly on patient care.

---

## Investment Strategies and Viable Business Models

* **Avoiding "Science Experiments":** Investors are shifting away from long-term, speculative biotechnology bets toward companies with clear, immediate paths to revenue.
    * **Direct-to-Clinician Sales:** Companies like Open Evidence bypass slow, low-margin B2B hospital procurement processes by selling AI-driven literature syntheses directly to doctors at the point of care.
    * **AI-Enabled Prescriptions:** Portfolio companies like Doctronic are legally executing automated medication refills and telemedicine routing in states like Utah, capturing direct transactional revenue.
* **Where Value Accrues:** On the services and technology side, value is generated directly inside the exam room where the patient-physician relationship is established. In biotech, physical therapeutic assets remain the ultimate currency, as major biopharma companies continue to focus on acquiring physical drugs rather than software platforms alone.

---

## Navigating Regulatory Windows and Data Oligopolies

* **A Pivotal Regulatory Window:** Bradley Tusk notes that while broad public and legislative sentiment toward AI has grown increasingly restrictive—such as New York considering a data center moratorium and federal executive orders targeting frontier models—the FDA and CMS remain highly innovative and permissive regarding healthcare AI.
    * **Urgency for Startups:** Companies requiring regulatory approvals should act rapidly, as shifting presidential administrations could pivot policies or roll back current clearances.
* **Overcoming the "EMR" Oligopoly:** Legacy Electronic Medical Record (EMR) systems like Epic remain highly fragmented and siloed, causing clinical bottlenecks and lost patient records.
* **The Rise of Consumer Health Records:** With the explosion of consumer wearables, personal genomic sequencing (now costing under $1,000), and accessible LLMs like Claude and OpenAI, consumers are increasingly building their own longitudinal health trackers, bypassing institutional data bottlenecks.
* **Balancing Privacy and Progress:** To achieve rapid drug breakthroughs and diagnostic systems, society may need to tolerate lower privacy thresholds. Many patient communities willingly share their health profiles to accelerate cures for rare diseases.

---

## The Next Frontier: Diagnostics, Trials, and AI Prescriptions

* **Computational Diagnostics:** AI's value lies in detecting patterns invisible to human clinicians. 
    * *Example:* Researchers are using routine mammography data to detect calcifications in arteries, identifying early-stage cardiovascular disease in women long before traditional symptoms manifest.
* **Real-Time Clinical Trials:** Traditional clinical trials suffer from severe data lags, often taking months to aggregate and clean data from international sites. Dr. Shalabh Gupta highlights the transition toward "digital twins" and real-time data analytics, which allows companies to monitor trial metrics instantly and terminate non-viable trials early to save capital.
* **The 3-Year Vision:** Panelists predict a future dominated by automated biometric-to-prescription systems, localized healthcare policies that integrate diagnostics with treatment, and the ubiquitous societal adoption of highly effective preventative therapies like GLP-1s.

---

## Notable Quotes

> "We have all this great technology and yet it’s sitting on the sidelines. If we just integrated the current technology we have, whether it be AI, genomics, therapeutics, diagnostics... I think we could unlock hundreds of millions of healthy life years for people around the world."
> — **Morgan Cheatham, M.D.**

> "Betting just on the promise of something, to me those are science experiments and I’m glad that somebody bets on them, but it’s usually not me."
> — **Bradley Tusk**

> "A lot of failure happens because we run trials that are the biggest part of the budget... Clinical trials is where these technologies can help... being able to see that in real time, it helps you make decisions faster, cut through the innovation trap, and also if things are not working, you can cut the trial off earlier."
> — **Shalabh Gupta, M.D.**

briefings.title: Why Secondary Markets Are Eating the IPO | All-In Liquidity Secondary Markets Panel
briefings.tldr: The secondary market has reached record volumes, doubling its 2021 peak to become a primary liquidity mechanism that actively competes with IPOs.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**  
The secondary market has reached record volumes, doubling its 2021 peak to become a primary liquidity mechanism that actively competes with IPOs. As companies choose to stay private longer, structured secondary markets are shifting from a shadow market into a highly regulated, democratized asset class, forcing venture capitalists to adopt active public-style selling strategies to return capital to LPs.

---

## ## The Exploding Scale of Secondary Markets
* **Record-Breaking Volume:** Secondary market transactions have reached record highs, doubling the previous peak observed at the end of 2021. 
* **Competing with Traditional Exits:** Employee and early investor secondaries now represent 31% of all primary venture activity in 2025, solidifying secondaries as a major alternative to traditional IPOs and M&A.
* **Shift to Premium Pricing:** In previous years, secondary shares traded at an average 20% discount (80 cents on the dollar) to incentivize buyers. By Q1 2025, secondary transactions surged to a premium of 106% of net asset value (NAV).
* **The Rise of "Quasi-Public" Giants:** Massive late-stage private companies—such as SpaceX, Anthropic, Anduril, and Databricks—now trade on secondary desks daily, effectively operating as public companies in terms of volume and interest without the associated regulatory disclosure burdens.

## ## The Debate on Staying Private vs. Going Public
* **The Danger of Private Market "Sycophancy":** Both Gavin Baker (Atreides) and Brad Gerstner (Altimeter) argue that staying private for too long harms executive decision-making. 
    * **Lack of Clean Feedback:** Private board members and investors often act as "sycophants," telling founders what they want to hear to protect their allocations for future rounds.
    * **Public Market Accountability:** Public markets provide immediate, rigorous, and unsentimental price discovery and pressure testing that forces management to execute cleanly.
* **The Mark Zuckerberg HTML5 Lesson:** Gavin Baker highlighted Facebook's historical 2010–2012 delay in building mobile native apps (relying too long on HTML5). Zuckerberg later reflected that had Facebook been public during that internal debate, rigorous questioning from public equity analysts would have forced him to correct the mistake years faster.
* **The Necessity of Liquidity for Talent:** With companies remaining private for decades (e.g., SpaceX for 24 years), employees frequently find themselves paper-rich but cash-poor. Structured liquidity programs are essential to allow early, hard-working employees to buy homes and support families without forcing the entire company into an premature IPO.

## ## Democratization and the Forge-Schwab Alliance
* **The Schwab Partnership:** Kelly Rodriques (CEO of Forge) detailed Forge’s landmark deal with Charles Schwab, which integrates Forge's private market trading infrastructure with Schwab’s 46 million retail accounts and $12 trillion in assets under management. 
* **Regulated Retail Access:** Private market access is rapidly evolving from high-fee, unregulated Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) toward regulated, diversified fund structures. 
    * **Interval and Closed-End Funds:** New fund products allow unaccredited retail investors to buy diversified private market baskets (featuring companies like SpaceX) with minimum investments as low as $500.
    * **Accreditation Changes:** Anticipated changes to SEC rules are expected to introduce a "sophisticated investor" test, replacing arbitrary wealth thresholds and further opening access to the private markets.
* **Systematizing Price Discovery:** Historically, secondary trading operated like a "ticket broker" grey market with fragmented bids. Forge is building an exchange-like infrastructure to provide clean, standardized price discovery for late-stage private equities.

## ## Active Portfolio Management and Venture Capital Exits
* **DPI Imperialism:** With LPs aggressively demanding Distributed to Paid-In Capital (DPI), venture capitalists can no longer afford to hold late-stage positions indefinitely. Brad Gerstner emphasized that Altimeter actively sells 30% to 40% slices of high-performing private positions at 4x or 5x valuations to return capital to LPs.
* **Crossover and Mutual Fund Constraints:** Large asset managers (like Fidelity, Wellington, and Baillie Gifford) are capped by SEC rules from holding more than 15% of their mutual funds in illiquid private assets (with most self-imposing stricter limits of 3% to 7%). 
    * **Unlocking Dry Powder:** When major private holdings finally go public and lockups expire, these assets move out of the restricted "private" bucket. This structural shift will unlock hundreds of billions of dollars in fresh, institutional late-stage demand.
* **Active Public-Style Discipline:** VCs must transition from a pure "buy and hold" mindset to active portfolio management, determining daily whether they should buy, hold, or sell, regardless of a company's private status.

## ## Top Late-Stage Private Targets of Interest
The panel highlighted several high-conviction private companies currently driving secondary interest:
* **Revolut:** Recommended by Chamath Palihapitiya as a premier European neo-bank built on a next-generation software stack. The company is actively unbundling incumbent banks, expanding rapidly in the US, and showing strong profitability across 14 lines of business.
* **Zipline:** A highly successful autonomous drone delivery network. The company achieved operational scale by delivering critical medical supplies in Africa—reducing maternal mortality by 90% to 95% in key regions—and is now successfully scaling commercial operations in the US.
* **Aria & DriveNets:** Highlighted by Gavin Baker as critical infrastructure plays. As AI data centers grow more specialized, these companies are rewriting the networking layer to synchronize disaggregated chips and coordinate prefill/decode processing workloads.
* **Sierra:** Co-founded by Bret Taylor and highlighted by Brad Gerstner. The company focuses on building sophisticated, agent-native customer service, sales, and marketing platforms.
* **Neural Robotics:** Highlighted by Kelly Rodriques as a German-based, AI-powered logistics robotics company that is quietly generating $100 million in revenue outside the Silicon Valley echo chamber.

---

## ## Notable Quotes

> "When you’re the CEO of a private company, you are the most special flower to all of your investors... Once a company’s public, you are one of thousands of companies and that’s its own dynamic. The consequence of this is that private investors are often selling to management teams. At some level, that can mean telling management teams what they need to hear because you want to keep participating in the rounds."  
> — **Gavin Baker**

> "I think we have a historic moment right now to get everybody into the game of capitalism... [But] I get worried at this point in the market cycles, particularly when you’re talking to retail investors at home. When people are telling you to YOLO into double-fee structure SPVs and all this, it’s time to be careful, to do your work, and to be thoughtful."  
> — **Brad Gerstner**

> "Being a private company CEO for most of my career and then being a public company CEO for three years, I recognize the job is incredibly different. It's much less fun... Turning into an investment manager primarily as a public company CEO is a very different job than being a visionary, product-first, first-principles business."  
> — **Kelly Rodriques**
